item.title: Xi urges new Mideast security steps
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-03
Xi urges new Mideast security steps President Xi Jinping called on Wednesday for efforts to build a new security architecture in the Middle East via upholding a vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security, while supporting countries in the region in developing good-neighborly and friendly relations. Xi made the remarks during talks with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi in Cairo, where he put forward a four-point proposal on the situation in the Middle East. Xi called for fostering the internal driving force for common security in the region, advancing an integrated approach, cementing development foundation and enhancing international coordination. Xi expressed opposition to interference by external forces and voiced support for countries in the region strengthening dialogue on peace and security, exploring the building of a new security architecture for the Middle East, and taking their future into their own hands. He said that a comprehensive approach should be adopted to advance common security in the region and that, given the multiple hot spots in the Middle East and their close interconnections, comprehensive solutions should be pursued. He stressed that the Palestinian question remains at the core of the Middle East issue and should never be ignored or marginalized. Development, Xi noted, is fundamental to achieving lasting peace and stability in the region. China stands ready to work with countries in the region to safeguard the security of international shipping lanes, advance development cooperation and promote the convergence of interests of the region's countries, thereby gradually enhancing mutual trust and eliminating the root causes of the conflict. Xi also said that international coordination for common security in the region should be strengthened, and the United Nations Charter and international law should serve as the fundamental principles for handling Middle East affairs. The international community, particularly major powers outside the region, should abandon double standards, respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of countries in the region and help safeguard regional peace and stability, he said, while calling for support for the UN in playing its due role in Middle East affairs. El-Sisi expressed high appreciation for China's consistent, objective and impartial positions on the Middle East issue. He reaffirmed Egypt's readiness to continue coordination with all regional and international parties, particularly with China, a pivotal state and a permanent member of the UN Security Council, in order to promote efforts aimed at reducing regional tensions, driving development and addressing global challenges. High-level talks Xi's two-day visit to Egypt marked his first state visit to Egypt in a decade and came as the two countries celebrate the 70th anniversary of diplomatic ties, with Egypt having been the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China. During his talks with El-Sisi, Xi noted that in recent years, under the joint guidance of the two leaders, the China-Egypt comprehensive strategic partnership has made significant strides. Amid a turbulent international and regional landscape, the two countries should continue supporting each other, deepen cooperation and advance the building of a China-Egypt community with a shared future, he stressed. Xi called on the two sides to maintain the momentum of high-level exchanges, expand communication and cooperation at various levels and in different fields, and strengthen exchanges and mutual learning on governance. Regarding economic cooperation, he urged stronger alignment of the two countries' development strategies and efforts to further tap the potential of traditional areas such as infrastructure, electricity, agriculture and communications technology. At the same time, the two countries should foster new areas of cooperation in green energy, electric vehicles, aerospace, the digital economy and modern agricultural technology, he said. Egypt was among the earliest countries to participate in Belt and Road cooperation. China has been Egypt's largest trading partner and source of imports for 14 consecutive years, while bilateral trade increased from $10.21 billion in 2013 to $20.79 billion in 2025. More than 2,800 Chinese companies are operating in Egypt, contributing to major projects in areas including infrastructure, new and renewable energy, transportation, economic zones, telecommunications, textiles, aerospace and advanced technologies, according to Khaled Nazmy, Egypt's ambassador to China. Xi also called for broader people-to-people exchanges in culture, education, science and technology, healthcare and sports, as well as greater personnel exchanges to strengthen mutual understanding between the two peoples. The two sides should deepen security cooperation, jointly combat transnational crime, strengthen international cooperation against corruption, firmly support each other's counterterrorism efforts, and safeguard their common security, he added. On multilateral affairs, Xi called for closer coordination within the UN, BRICS and other multilateral platforms, as well as joint efforts to promote the development of the China-Arab States Cooperation Forum and the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation. The two countries should work together to oppose unilateralism and bullying and promote a more just and equitable global governance system, he added. El-Sisi reaffirmed Egypt's firm adherence to the one-China principle and hailed the "tangible leap" in bilateral relations across various fields, saying there is clear political will on both sides to further expand cooperation, particularly in industrial localization and technology transfer. Following the talks, the two presidents witnessed the signing of a number of cooperation documents covering Belt and Road cooperation, artificial intelligence, trade and economic cooperation, and industrial and supply chains. The two sides also issued a joint statement on further deepening their comprehensive strategic partnership. More than 20 cooperation documents were signed during the visit in areas including the digital economy, science and technology, education and transportation.

item.title: Visit was amazing, says former US teacher
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-02
Visit was amazing, says former US teacher Retired United States teacher Ronald Sakolsky said his 10-day visit to China has far exceeded anything he could have imagined, as he witnessed the country's environmental progress and reconnected with former students who now have professionally established careers. He visited China from Aug 23 to Tuesday at the invitation of the China Education Association for International Exchange. The story of Sakolsky and desert greening pioneer Yin Yuzhen from the Inner Mongolia autonomous region has sparked wide discussion online, turning both of them into well-known figures in China. In 1999, Sakolsky helped Yin's greening efforts with a $5,000 donation, which has since helped contribute to the planting of more than 50,000 trees. "I did not have expectations when I came back to China," Sakolsky said in an interview with China Daily on Tuesday. "This journey for the last 10 days has been beyond what I even could have expected." Sakolsky, who taught in China through a teacher exchange program in Luoyang, Henan province, from 1999 to 2000, expressed amazement at the changes in cities and air quality. "The advancement just has been amazing to me. Luoyang is a beautiful, beautiful city. They've made it a beautiful city, but you know what? They didn't stop; they're still building." He repeatedly turned the spotlight away from himself and onto Yin. "She proved me wrong and made it possible," he said. "She's the one who carried the trees on her shoulder, dug into the sand to plant them, and watered them; she's the hero," he added. Sakolsky stressed that the core message is not about any individual, but about protecting the planet. "I'm not the spotlight. The story is not me. The message is that students come first. Plant a tree. Mother Earth is alive. We must take care of the earth so that she will take care of us," he said. Sakolsky emphasized the need for greater mutual understanding between China and the US. He noted that many Americans have limited knowledge about China due to a lack of education on the subject. Similarly, he mentioned that many Chinese people have insufficient information about the US. "Through education, teacher exchange, student exchange … we can educate those who wish to learn and bring us closer together." When asked whether the idea of China and the US becoming like family is too idealistic, he pointed to Yin's example: the impossible can become possible. He acknowledged that achieving closer ties would take a long time and happen very slowly, but he insisted that progress must be made and that the two countries should move forward rather than backward. He also encouraged young people in both countries to broaden their perspectives, noting that many Americans mistakenly believe the rest of the world lives as they do. He pointed out that different nations have their own ways of life, and that by learning from one another and adopting the best from each, the world could become a better place. Yang Jun, vice-president and secretary-general of the China Education Association for International Exchange, said that the simple act of kindness Sakolsky showed 26 years ago has resulted in a lifelong friendship. He expressed hope that the seeds planted today would grow into millions of such relationships. Yang added that Sakolsky's story demonstrates that a successful program can yield a friendship that spans decades, a forest that spans acres and a role model that inspires millions.

item.title: China sends second batch of emergency aid to Nepal
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-02
China sends second batch of emergency aid to Nepal China's second batch of emergency humanitarian aid for Nepal's mudslide relief efforts arrived in Kathmandu on Tuesday, following devastating mudslides triggered by a glacier collapse on Aug 26. The shipment weighed about 5.8 metric tons and included urgently needed supplies such as water purification and lighting equipment, genetic testing equipment and drones, according to Luo Feiyu, a staff member with the China International Center for Economic and Technical Exchanges under the Ministry of Commerce. The supplies were urgently sourced, consolidated and transported overnight through coordination between the Foreign Ministry, the Ministry of Commerce, the General Administration of Customs, the China International Development Cooperation Agency and other departments, Luo said. Five experts from Shenzhen also departed for the disaster-hit areas in Nepal on Tuesday. Chinese DNA identification experts will also travel to the affected areas to assist Nepal with its relief efforts, Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a regular news conference on Tuesday. A sudden glacier collapse in Nepal's border area on Aug 26 triggered severe mudslides, causing significant casualties and leaving many people missing in both China and Nepal. According to the latest figures as of 1 pm on Tuesday from Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the death toll had risen to 1,003, while 3,916 people remained missing. As rescue and relief operations continued on the Chinese side of the border, China moved quickly to provide emergency assistance to Nepal. China has provided $2 million in emergency cash assistance to the Nepalese government, while the Red Cross Society of China has provided $200,000 to Nepal's Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund, according to the Chinese embassy in Nepal. The first batch of 13,200 relief items, weighing 50 tons and including tents, blankets, sleeping bags, compressed food and first-aid kits, arrived in Kathmandu on Sunday. Two teams of Chinese tunnel rescue experts have also reached the disaster-hit areas in Nepal. "Providing emergency assistance to the disaster-hit areas in Nepal and carrying out international rescue cooperation is an important political decision made by China and reflects China's friendship with Nepal," Guo said at a news conference on Tuesday. He noted that China and Nepal have long maintained sound cooperation in meteorology, water resources and disaster prevention and mitigation. "Since the disaster occurred, China and Nepal have maintained smooth communication on personnel search and rescue, information sharing and the prevention of secondary disasters. China has continued to provide Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data, conduct professional consultations and provide relevant early-warning information," he said. China will continue to support Nepal's disaster relief efforts and deepen cooperation with the country in disaster prevention and mitigation to safeguard the shared interests of the two peoples, he added. zhaojia@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Live: Road access to mudslide-hit border port restored
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-02
President Xi Jinping urges all-out rescue, relief efforts after mudslide hits border port in Xizang Level-II emergency response activated after mudslide hits border port in Xizang Rescue teams are intensifying deep searches in the core disaster area around Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, where mudslide deposits reach up to 16 meters in some places. The main land route into the area was largely restored on Wednesday morning. Follow live updates from China Daily's on-site reports. Chinese meteorological and water authorities have stepped up cooperation with Nepal following the deadly mudslide that struck the China-Nepal border, sharing monitoring data and providing weather and hydrological forecasts to support rescue efforts. The Aug 26 disaster originated on the Nepalese side of the border and severely affected Gyirong Port in the Xizang autonomous region. The area's high altitude, complex terrain and rapidly changing weather conditions have made rescue operations particularly challenging. "From late August to early September, plateau shear lines and low vortices are frequently active along the border, with frequent precipitation, posing serious challenges to rescue work," said Ma Xuekuan, chief forecaster at the National Meteorological Center. Following a request from Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology around noon on Aug 26, the China Meteorological Administration organized an emergency joint consultation with its Nepalese counterpart that afternoon. A second consultation was held on Aug 31, according to Zhang Tianhang, a senior engineer at the World Meteorological Center, Beijing. The two sides also established a WeChat working group for real-time information sharing, allowing them to respond quickly to requests during the emergency. The consultations used MAZU, a cloud-based early warning system, to jointly assess weather conditions and forecast precipitation in the affected area. China subsequently established a dedicated meteorological support team for Nepal and began providing daily monitoring and forecasting reports in English. "Overall, we have provided seamless forecasting services covering the next 30 days, offering strong support for Nepal's rescue operations," Zhang said. China has also provided Nepal with a customized version of MAZU. Nepal has since requested additional functions, including lightning monitoring, subseasonal-to-seasonal forecasts and more detailed monitoring and forecasting products. Chinese authorities have shared a range of meteorological products and observation data through the customized version of MAZU, Zhang said. Water authorities have also joined the effort. A barrier lake formed near the confluence of Nepal's Cuojian River and China's Purepu Tsangpo River following the disaster. The Ministry of Water Resources immediately sent a hydrological emergency monitoring team to the area, working with Xizang's regional hydrological and water resources survey authorities. Chinese authorities are providing Nepal with daily updates in five areas, including the development of the barrier lake; potential chain risks from impact pits along the Cuojian River; risks from glacial lakes in the Gyirong Zangbo basin; the development and risk forecasts of newly formed barrier lakes; and emergency hydrological monitoring information. The information is intended to help Nepal assess risks and organize rescue efforts downstream, according to the ministry. Following the disaster, the CMA mobilized resources from the national to local levels. A small ground weather station was installed near the disaster area on the night of Aug 26, and a mobile weather radar was deployed nearby on Sept 1. "These facilities have supplemented our understanding of local weather conditions and improved the precision and accuracy of local forecasts," Ma said. Rescue teams at Gyirong Port in the Xizang autonomous region will maintain round-the-clock searches in the core disaster area while adjusting deployments as risks evolve and strengthening monitoring of secondary disasters, evacuation planning and logistical support, regional authorities said on Wednesday. Wang Haitao, head of the Xizang Fire and Rescue Corps, said at a news conference that high-altitude protection and psychological support for rescuers would also be strengthened. As of noon on Wednesday, 21 victims had been found, 847 personal belongings had been recovered and 541 people remained missing. The mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, on Aug 26 after originating on the Nepalese side of the China-Nepal border. It cut off roads to the hardest-hit area and exposed rescuers to steep terrain, deep mud and the risks of rockfalls, landslides and barrier lakes. Before the main land route was restored, fire and rescue teams used coordinated land, water and air operations to reach the disaster zone, Wang said. An advance team descended more than 500 meters by rope and reached the core area at 4:30 pm on Aug 28, where it established a forward command post. Rescuers then divided the area into grids and conducted repeated searches using manual excavation, search dogs, detection equipment and machinery. Waterborne teams searched riverbanks and sediment-filled sections, while drones conducted reconnaissance and helicopters supported personnel rotation and supply deliveries. With road access restored, operations have shifted from reaching the core area to conducting deeper searches. An additional 65 firefighters and more than 200 pieces of equipment have joined an initial force of 24 rescuers and two search dogs. Teams are now searching from the surface into deeper debris, focusing on areas around the border gate, collapsed structures, thick mud deposits, river valleys and other hard-to-reach locations. Fire and rescue teams are mainly responsible for two key areas — the customs accommodation building and a parking lot. A 195-member task force has been divided into three rotating groups to conduct layer-by-layer searches, clearing debris and checking each newly exposed section before moving deeper. Large machinery is being used to open up working areas, while firefighters, search dogs and detection equipment conduct more precise searches. Geological and water resources experts are continuing real-time risk assessments, while teams monitor landslides, barrier lakes and other potential secondary hazards. Wang said rescue forces would continue adjusting deployments, maintaining day-and-night shifts, refining evacuation plans and coordinating heavy machinery and helicopter support. They will also strengthen logistical support, personal protection and psychological services for rescuers engaged in prolonged operations. Rescue teams are intensifying deep searches in the core disaster area around Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, where mudslide deposits reach up to 16 meters in some places. The main land route into the area was largely restored on Wednesday morning, regional authorities reported. As of noon Wednesday, 21 people had been found dead and 541 remained missing, according to Karma Tsetan, chairman of the Xizang regional government. Additionally, 847 personal belongings have been recovered. Originating on the Nepalese side of the China-Nepal border, the mudslide struck Gyirong Port on Aug 26, severing roads, electricity, and communications. Karma Tsetan stated that over 2,300 rescuers had been mobilized, supported by more than 400 vehicle deployments and over 8,000 sets of rescue equipment. Drones have conducted 804 flights, while 5.43 metric tons of supplies and equipment have been air-dropped into the core area. Prior to the restoration of the land route, rescuers advanced by water, land, and air. Boats approached the core zone via waterways, land teams trekked for about 12 hours along mountain routes, and helicopters made 24 flights to transport rescuers and supplies. Communications have improved with 12 base stations restored, and lighting and power equipment deployed in the core area, Karma Tsetan said. Rescuers have conducted repeated grid searches covering about 1.59 million square meters since the disaster. More than 10 pieces of heavy machinery have now entered the core area to support deeper searches. Reopening National Highway G216 was a major priority. Karma Tsetan noted that rescue teams worked tirelessly despite narrow working areas, unstable slopes, fast-rising water, deep mud, and continued rainfall. Rescue forces will continue coordinating searches, road restoration, recovery work, and risk prevention as operations progress deeper into the disaster zone, he said. Ren Wei, executive vice-chairman of the Xizang regional government, said search operations are now focusing on deeper layers of debris. Mudslide deposits in the core area average about 4 meters in depth, reaching up to 16 meters in some places, with large rocks and thick mud covering the surface. Rescuers have divided the area into sections and are using professional detection equipment to search beneath the debris. Priority is given to key locations, including a parking lot, the joint inspection building, and accommodation buildings. As searches move deeper, authorities are enhancing precautions against secondary disasters. Rockfall radar, slope radar, and other equipment are monitoring surrounding mountains, gullies, and debris deposits around the clock, while meteorological authorities provide detailed forecasts every six hours. Each search site has a dedicated safety officer, with evacuation signals, escape routes, and safe assembly areas prepared in advance. Ren said remains found during searches are being transferred and identified, while recovered personal belongings are catalogued, preserved, and handed over according to established procedures. Health and sanitation measures are also ongoing in the affected area. Moderate rainfall was forecast for the mudslide-devastated Gyirong Port area in China's Xizang autonomous region on Wednesday as rescue efforts proceed in the wake of the deadly natural disaster along the China-Nepal border, with major hidden risks still present in nearby watercourses. The total accumulated precipitation is expected to reach 30 to 50 millimeters, with rainfall expected to last until Friday, the ministry said in a media release on Wednesday. It said the rainfall is likely to push up water levels along the Gyirong Tsangpo River, raising the flow rate in the Gyirong Port section of the watercourse to about 150 to 300 cubic meters per second. The ministry didn't disclose the current flow rate in the section, but said a monitoring station 7 kilometers upstream of the port stood at 91.7 cubic meters per second at 1 pm on Wednesday. The ministry urged frontline rescue personnel in the area to closely monitor real-time rainfall and changes in river conditions. Workers were advised to prepare in advance for evacuation and flood-risk mitigation. The ministry warned that, based on consistent drone monitoring and satellite imagery analysis, there remain major hidden risks around the mudslide-stricken area. It said glaciers around a nearby scour pit in Nepal's Chhochen Khola River, which converges with the Purepu Tsangpo River in China, face potential collapse. It said small-scale landslides have been detected along the downstream reach of a barrier lake on the Purepu Tsangpo, heightening the risk of slope collapse that may form new barrier lakes. According to authorities, the mudslide originating in Nepal has left 21 dead and 541 missing in the port. In the aftermath of the mudslide that struck Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, psychological support for the families of the deceased and missing, as well as local residents and rescue workers, has been prioritized, officials announced on Wednesday. Following the landslide on Aug 26, Shigatse authorities swiftly formed a response team and developed a comprehensive plan to manage the aftermath, proactively reaching out to the families of the missing, according to Wang Fanghong, deputy head of the disaster emergency and rescue command headquarters and Party secretary of Shigatse. So far, 587 family members of missing or deceased individuals have been accommodated and assisted, Wang revealed. A team of 70 professionals has been assigned to provide psychological counseling to these families, offering care and assistance 1,107 times. Additionally, 1,220 personnel have been organized to support these services, according to him. Four dedicated phone lines have also been established to offer consultation services to families of missing and deceased individuals both domestically and internationally. These lines have received 876 calls — 448 from China and 428 from abroad — with all inquiries documented for follow-up responses, Wang said. "Ongoing care and support will be provided to the families of the deceased and missing," he added. Tan Xiangdong, Party chief of the Xizang autonomous regional health commission, emphasized the importance of psychological support, acknowledging the deep trauma caused by the mudslide. "We have prioritized psychological support by developing plans for counseling and crisis intervention," he said, noting tailored mental health services are being provided to address the specific needs of different affected groups. In collaboration with the National Health Commission and other provinces and cities, over 210 psychological assistance experts have been selected and are on standby to respond to the needs of the disaster-stricken areas, ensuring the sustainability of psychological aid, he said. Local medical professionals, particularly Tibetan doctors, have been leveraged, and specialists with strong foreign language skills have been appointed to communicate with the families of missing foreign nationals, he added. Psychological support is also being provided to local residents and rescue workers. At each disaster relocation site, Tan said, at least four medical staff have been assigned to ensure the presence of healthcare professionals, disease control personnel, mobile medical services, medication availability, and psychological care. "A bilingual Chinese-Tibetan pocket guide for psychological self-help has been developed to address various post-disaster stress reactions," he specified. "Interventions are conducted through listening, companionship, guidance, and comfort, with one-on-one interventions and continuous follow-ups provided for specific families." As of Wednesday noon, a total of 966 psychological comfort and emotional support sessions have been conducted for the residents at the relocation sites, he revealed. For rescue workers, psychological risk assessments are conducted promptly, providing necessary group and individual counseling. A pocket guide for psychological self-help specifically for frontline rescue workers has been developed to help them understand emergency responses and how to manage them, he said, adding that a hotline — 12356 — has also been established for psychological services. Authorities in the Xizang autonomous region have intensified monitoring and early warning efforts against secondary disasters following the recent mudslide at Gyirong Port, deploying experts and specialized equipment to guard against further collapses, landslides and debris flows. Karma Tsetan, chairman of the regional government and head of the emergency rescue headquarters, said 93 experts and technical personnel are monitoring the barrier lake and the source area of the ice-rock avalanche. Geological hazards along roads leading to the border port are also being investigated, while rainfall, temperature and water-level changes in key river basins are being closely monitored to protect rescue personnel downstream. The barrier lake had discharged naturally by Aug 30, removing the immediate threat, while a small body of water formed by the ice-rock avalanche had also drained, Karma Tsetan said. About 150 sets of specialized equipment have been deployed, including 104 sets of radar, video surveillance, drones, and hydrological and meteorological monitoring devices. The Aug 26 disaster had left 21 people dead and 541 missing as of Wednesday noon. Chen Fuqi, chief engineer of the regional Department of Natural Resources, said the area's steep terrain, complex geological conditions and high-altitude hazard sources make early detection difficult. Authorities will integrate satellite remote sensing, drone surveys and ground monitoring, while strengthening geological hazard surveys, early warning, emergency coordination and cross-border information sharing, Chen said. Twenty-one people have been confirmed dead and 541 others remain missing as of 12 pm Wednesday after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in China's Xizang autonomous region on Aug 26. Additionally, 847 personal belongings have been found. Road access to the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region was nearly restored at 10:00 am on Wednesday after days of around-the-clock repair work on the damaged G216 national highway. Fire and rescue forces have optimized deployment to enhance search-and-rescue efficiency in the area. On Aug 29, a catering support vehicle from the Red Cross Society of the Xizang Autonomous Region arrived in Gyirong town to provide meal support for frontline medical staff, cargo handlers and sanitation workers. After completing food distribution at Gyirong Port Hospital on Sept 2, teams drove to workers' rest areas to deliver hot meals. Though simple, these meals serve as solid backing for ongoing mudslide relief efforts. More rain is forecast for Gyirong county in the Xizang autonomous region over the next three days, prompting authorities to closely monitor river levels, road conditions and the risk of secondary disasters as rescue crews continue working at the site of a deadly mudslide. The county is typically in the latter part of its rainy season in early September, seeing frequent cloudy and rainy weather and a tendency for rainfall at night, said Huang Zhuo, deputy director of the National Meteorological Center. "Localized precipitation could be heavier in the low-elevation river valleys in southern Gyirong," he said. Light to moderate rain is expected on Wednesday and Thursday, followed by cloudy to overcast conditions with showers on Friday. Most of the rainfall is expected at night, Huang said. Temperatures in Gyirong are forecast to range from highs of about 21 to 24 C to lows of 13 to 15 C. The weather outlook has direct implications for rescue teams working around the disaster site. Rain could leave roads slippery along the routes from Shigatse to Gyirong Port, requiring drivers and rescue crews to exercise caution. Authorities advised rescuers to closely monitor fluctuations in water levels around the disaster area and keep personnel and heavy machinery away from low-lying areas at night. Since the mudslide disaster occurred in Gyirong county, meteorological authorities have intensified weather observations and deployed artificial intelligence forecasting to closely track changing conditions, said Wang Yawei, spokesman for the China Meteorological Administration. Meteorological departments at all levels have also established teams on the ground and divided responsibilities for emergency weather services, Wang said. "We are providing real-time information on weather trends in and around the disaster area, forecasts along transportation routes, aviation weather conditions, rainfall over the barrier lake and weather-related risks from potential secondary disasters," he said. Meteorological authorities have also begun working with their counterparts in Nepal. "We contacted Nepal's meteorological agency shortly after the disaster and began video consultations on weather conditions. China has provided Nepal with a customized version of its MAZU intelligent early-warning platform soon after the disaster, which supplies meteorological monitoring, forecasts and early warnings. The system integrates data from Fengyun meteorological satellites and ground-based observation networks and incorporates artificial intelligence weather forecasting models, providing meteorological support for Nepal's rescue and emergency response efforts, Wang said. They also plan to expand scientific research on climate change and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, including changes in permafrost, snow cover and glaciers under a warming climate, in an effort to improve scientific support for future disaster prevention and response, he added. Road access to the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in Xizang was basically restored on Wednesday after days of round-the-clock repair work on the damaged G216 national highway. Armed police officer Zhang Jian, working on the frontline of the Gyirong rescue operation, shares the challenges facing rescuers at the disaster site. Large rescue machinery has reached the core disaster area at Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, following the completion of a temporary roadbed across the last water-damaged section of National Highway G216. This marks a significant advancement in ongoing search and rescue operations. The highway, the main route to the port, was severed after a massive mudslide from the Nepalese side of the China-Nepal border struck the area on Aug 26, resulting in major casualties and leaving many people missing. Rescue, relief, and recovery efforts are actively underway, with road reopening and searches for missing individuals progressing simultaneously. After overnight repairs, crews completed a temporary roadbed at the final section of G216 where the roadway had been washed out, enabling large machinery to access the disaster-hit core area. Rescuers are working to reinforce the section so that smaller vehicles can also use the route, further enhancing access for personnel, supplies, and equipment. Rescue workers reached the core area on foot on Tuesday night, and by Wednesday morning, numerous excavators and other heavy machines had been deployed to the area. Multiple pieces of heavy equipment are now operational around Gyirong Port, aiding in the search for missing people while also clearing and leveling damaged roads. Authorities report that various search methods are being employed in the core disaster zone as rescue teams persist in their efforts to locate the missing and restore access through the affected area. GYIRONG, Xizang -- Road access to the core area of the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region was basically restored at 10 am on Wednesday after days of round-the-clock repair work on the damaged G216 national highway. Rescue teams, relief supplies and some rescue equipment have entered the core rescue area via this road, rescuers said. A section of the G216 national highway, the only land route to Gyirong Port, was severely damaged by the mudslide carrying huge boulders, with the restoration of road access critically important in aiding large-scale search operations in the core disaster area. The repair operation, notably, posed formidable challenges. "Conditions vary from one section of the road to another," said Zhou Gang from China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise. The original roadbed remained usable in some sections, but most of it had been severely damaged. The work zone lay in a narrow mountain gorge, with steep mountainsides on one side and a fast-flowing river on the other. This confined space made it difficult for multiple pieces of heavy machinery to operate simultaneously, severely hampering the work, Zhou added. An even greater challenge came from the unpredictable conditions inside the gorge, featuring fast-flowing water and lingering risks of rockfalls, landslides and other secondary hazards. Crews responded by adapting their methods. Along narrow sections, multiple excavators worked in relay, lining up one behind another to dig and pass debris from one machine to the next. In sections with the strongest currents, excavators pushed into the water to open the way, while crews built diversion structures and used rock-filled steel cages to stabilize the roadbed, advancing section by section. The mudslide, caused by an ice-rock avalanche in Nepal, hit Gyirong Port on Aug 26, claiming 16 lives and leaving 546 people missing at the border port as of 6 pm on Saturday, according to the regional government's latest update. Following the disaster, Xizang swiftly activated its highest-level emergency response for natural disasters, mobilizing rescue forces from across the region for search and rescue operations, road clearance and other relief work in Gyirong. A deadly mudslide, caused by an ice-rock avalanche in Nepal on Aug 26 led to interruption of roads, communication and power around the Gyirong Port in Gyirong county, Xizang autonomous region. Saleb township of the county is close to the source of this mudslide disaster, and residents of three villages in the township have been quickly evacuated to safe areas after the disaster. However, the villagers are worried about their poultry, livestock and farmland. Rescuers from the Saleb township went to the evacuated villages at regular intervals every day to help the villagers feed their poultry and livestock, patrol the villages, and safeguard their property. By the time Phuntsok Drakpa sat down to talk about the rescue operation at Gyirong Port in the Xizang autonomous region on Tuesday, he still had not dealt with the insect that had burrowed into his skin days earlier. He had more urgent things to do. Phuntsok Drakpa, an officer at a community police station in Gyirong county, immediately volunteered to join the search-and-rescue effort after a deadly mudslide struck the port on Aug 26. The journey from Lapher village, where his police station is located, to the port was not a road in the conventional sense. Much of it was a narrow trail cut into the mountainside, with a cliff on one side and a drop so deep that the bottom could not be seen, he said. In some places, there was no trail at all. The officers had to push through dense brush, cutting branches, thorny vines and weeds to make their way forward. About 1.5 kilometers from the port, they reached the most dangerous section: a valley more than 200 meters deep, with slopes of 60 to 70 degrees. "Some sections were bare rock. Others were wet and slippery from the rain. We had to use ropes to lower ourselves down," he said. Phuntsok Drakpa had one thought as he moved: Get there as quickly as possible. "If we arrived one minute earlier, there could be one more chance," he said. The officers traveled about 7.7 km on foot. About 5.5 km could be covered at a slow jog, while the rest was so difficult to traverse that it consumed most of their time. The journey lasted more than 10 hours. They left at 9 am on Saturday and returned by helicopter the following morning, he recalled. The mountain posed hazards beyond the disaster itself. There were leeches and poisonous snakes, as well as insects that lived in pine trees. One of them had burrowed into his skin, leaving a wound he was still carrying when he gave the interview. The officers covered themselves as tightly as they could, fastening the cuffs of their uniforms to keep the insects out. They slept together outdoors along the route. When they woke the next morning, they found a bear's paw print about two meters from where they had been sleeping. "At the time, nobody had time to be frightened. We simply kept moving," he said. From 9 am one day until noon the next, the officers ate nothing. At one point, they encountered firefighters and gave much of their food to them. "Yet I did not feel hungry," he said. They spent a night in the rain. He did not feel cold, either, though he knew that under normal circumstances he would have. Once they arrived at the port, the task became harder to describe. "The air smelled of decay. The site was completely quiet, without any sound." The officers searched among the rocks, calling out and looking for any sign that someone might be trapped beneath them — a shoe, a piece of clothing, anything that might suggest where a person was. "It was very difficult," Phuntsok Drakpa said. "There was nothing we could do except call out and look under the rocks." If they found something, they dug. Sometimes, all they could do was cry, he said. But there was no time to dwell on what they had seen. After the interview, Phuntsok Drakpa planned to head to Salhe township, taking the same mountain route again. He still had not dealt with the insect in his skin. "I plan to buy some insecticide and spray it so that the insect will come out on its own," he said. Contact the writers at zhaoyimeng@chinadaily.com.cn For Tashi Norbu's 61-year-old father from Lapher village in Gyirong county, Xizang autonomous region, starting the day with tsampa — roasted barley flour mixed with yak butter and tea — does more than nourish the body. It soothes the heart and sets a peaceful tone for the day ahead. So when Tashi Norbu and his family were relocated to Jephuk village following the mudslide that struck the Gyirong border port on Aug 26, they found comfort in the familiar food provided at their temporary shelter, as well as in the free accommodation. "The streets here are narrower and the houses are closer together than at our home. But the altitude of Jephuk village is similar to that of our village, so we adapted to the new environment pretty quickly," he said. About 160 villagers from Lapher and Sichung have been resettled in rural homestays in Jephuk village, a popular tourist destination with dozens of guesthouses and restaurants. "My father felt carsick at first during the bumpy ride here, but he feels much better after seeing a doctor arranged by relief workers and volunteers," Tashi Norbu said. "The restaurant near our temporary home sometimes brings Tibetan noodle soup to our door in the morning as a gesture of kindness." "Despite the disaster, we feel well taken care of," he said. According to local authorities, 499 residents from five affected villages have been relocated to five temporary shelters converted from hotels and homestays following the devastating mudslide. Jampal Dorje, a staff member at the shelter in Jephuk village, said many of the relocated residents are elderly and have been housed with their children to ensure they receive proper care. "Most elderly residents are not used to rice and steamed buns included in the standard food supplies, so we have requested more tsampa, Tibetan fried noodles and dumplings from the supply reserves in recent days," he said. Jampal Dorje said staff members now visit households every day to keep track of residents' needs, paying particular attention to their health, sleep quality and other basic daily necessities. Several medical workers are stationed at the shelter to provide care, while designated vehicles are available to transport residents with more serious symptoms to hospitals, he said. At a hotel-turned-shelter, Dawa, a doctor from Shigatse Tibetan Medicine Hospital, said she has brought Tibetan incense and offered counseling sessions to help residents struggling with emotional distress. In more severe cases, relatives of people who remain missing have fainted and required oxygen therapy, she said. Karsang Tenjen Tamang, a Nepali who operates a restaurant in Jephuk village, has also opened his establishment as a place for displaced villagers and relief workers to rest. "The government provides free meals and housing for affected residents every day. They are being well looked after here," he said. Contact the writers at wangxiaoyu@chinadaily.com.cn Rescuers are intensifying search operations around Gyirong Port while working to reopen the main ground route to the disaster-hit area, as difficult terrain, heavy rainfall and the risk of secondary disasters continue to complicate rescue efforts. As of 6 pm on Tuesday, crews clearing National Highway G216 had advanced to within 700 meters of fully reopening the route. The highway was severely damaged by a massive mudslide that struck the area on Aug 26 after originating on the Nepalese side of the China-Nepal border. The disaster caused major casualties and left many people missing, while roads, electricity and communications were also disrupted. On Tuesday morning, memorial ceremonies for the victims were held at the core rescue area and road-clearing sites near Gyirong Port, attended by rescuers, local officials and residents. Norbu Tsering, acting mayor of Shigatse, said rescuers had spent four consecutive days searching about 0.7 square kilometers around the border gate using life-detection equipment and other methods. "The priority remains reopening the road to the border gate while further intensifying the search in the core area," he said. Search operations are advancing from both directions. Firefighters are moving from the outer edge of the debris field toward Gyirong Port, while teams in the core area are searching outward. A stretch of about 2 km has so far been searched from the outer edge toward the port. Nearly 700 personnel and more than 300 sets of machinery have been involved in restoring the land route, while supplies and additional rescue forces are being sent into the core area by air. Large machinery is also advancing toward the core area along G216. Thubten Nyima, a firefighter with the Xizang fire and rescue brigade, said firefighters are preparing to combine mechanized excavation with more detailed manual searches once heavy equipment reaches areas where deeper debris cannot be effectively searched by hand. The same terrain that amplified the mudslide's destructive force is now hampering rescue work. Experts said the disaster's impact was intensified by the steep elevation drop, high speed and narrow valley. The debris flow traveled about 22 km at an average speed of around 50 meters per second, gathering loose material as it descended. Heavy machinery can only advance along the narrow valley, while search, road repair and debris-clearing teams must share the same confined corridor. Thubten Nyima said reaching the core area had already placed heavy physical demands on rescuers, while damaged transportation and communications infrastructure created further difficulties. Deep mud has slowed movement and reduced the effectiveness of some commonly used detection equipment. The mud in some areas is knee-or even waist-deep, he said. Teams have had to identify relatively stable routes and adjust search plans according to terrain, weather conditions and the likely direction of the mudslide. Rain can further complicate operations, requiring plans to be continuously adjusted. Conditions along G216 remain difficult, with unstable cliffs on one side and fast-flowing water on the other. Currents reach 6 to 7 meters per second in some sections. Lin Zhenkui, a technical expert with China Anneng Group, told CCTV that the mudslide raised the riverbed and altered the channel, forcing water onto parts of the former roadway. In some sections, crews are effectively building a new road through the water rather than simply clearing debris. Large rocks, reinforced stone cages and diversion structures are being used to stabilize the roadbed and reduce the force of the current. Communications and power supplies are also being restored. As of 5 pm on Tuesday, telecommunications operators had repaired one damaged base station and set up 12 emergency stations, according to the regional communications administration. State Grid said power crews were working around the clock to support road-clearing operations, with power lines extended to within 1.6 km of Gyirong Port. Secondary hazards remain a major concern. Three national emergency rescue teams totaling 39 personnel have been deployed with slope radar, drones and life-detection equipment to monitor potential landslides, collapses and barrier lakes, according to the Ministry of Emergency Management. China Anneng Group is also using laser-based video, artificial intelligence monitoring equipment and drones to track slope changes around the clock. The Ministry of Water Resources said on Tuesday that 14 previously identified glacial lakes remained relatively stable, though glaciers around an impact crater near the source area in Nepal could still collapse, posing a significant risk. Three rope-ladder evacuation routes totaling about 180 meters have also been installed along G216, allowing rescuers to reach higher ground quickly in the event of sudden flooding or another mudslide. Norbu Tsering said authorities are maintaining contact with the families of those missing and providing updates on rescue efforts. KATHMANDU -- Another batch of Chinese relief supplies and experts arrived in Kathmandu, Nepal, by air on Tuesday, as part of Chinese aid efforts following the deadly mudslide on Wednesday. Tailored to Nepal's on-the-ground needs, the aid package includes urgently required items such as drones, DNA testing devices and reagents, water-purification equipment, and lighting gear. The aid came after China sent its first batch of relief supplies to Nepal on Sunday. Five DNA identification specialists, forming the third team of Chinese aid experts for Nepal, were on the same flight. Upon their arrival, the Chinese DNA identification experts headed straight to the disaster-hit areas to assist Nepalese authorities with relief operations. Nepalese authorities said Tuesday that the death toll from the massive mudslide had risen to 1,068, with 4,606 people still missing.

item.title: Peng Liyuan chats over tea with wife of Egyptian president
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-02
Peng Liyuan chats over tea, visits exhibition with wife of Egyptian president CAIRO -- Peng Liyuan, wife of President Xi Jinping, chatted over tea and visited a small handicrafts exhibition with Entissar El-Sisi, wife of Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi, on Wednesday. Peng had a cordial exchange with Entissar on China-Egypt friendship and people-to-people exchanges. Egypt has a long history and a profound cultural heritage, Peng said, noting that the exquisite exhibits fully showcased the wisdom and unique aesthetic sensibilities of the Egyptian people. China and Egypt share many cultural similarities, Peng said, expressing hope that artists from the two countries would strengthen exchanges and cooperation to allow traditional crafts to continue to shine with renewed vitality through inheritance and mutual learning.

item.title: Equal, orderly multipolar world urged
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-02
Equal, orderly multipolar world urged President Xi Jinping called on Tuesday for joint efforts to advance an equal and orderly multipolar world and make global governance more just and equitable, saying that Global South countries should have greater representation and a stronger voice in international affairs. Xi made the remarks at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Plus Meeting in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, which focused on strengthening the role of the United Nations and building a multipolar world. Against the backdrop of accelerating changes unseen in a century, Xi said that hegemonism, unilateralism and protectionism are resurging against historical trends. Nevertheless, the overwhelming majority of the world does not condone power politics, conflict and confrontation, or isolation and backwardness, he said, adding that what most people want instead is to hold a place on the world stage through national development and international cooperation. Noting that the rise of the Global South is driving a profound shift in the international balance of power, Xi said that the trend toward a multipolar world is irreversible. "As a responsible major country, China advocates for an equal and orderly multipolar world," he said. The Chinese president identified sovereign equality and mutual respect as fundamental principles, balance, order and the rule of law as inherent requirements, multilateralism, dialogue and consultation as essential pathways, and mutual benefit, win-win cooperation and inclusiveness as the way forward for development. "We should ensure equal rights, equal opportunities and equal rules for all countries, regardless of their size, strength and wealth," Xi said. The common values of humanity should be upheld, while double standards, exceptionalism, foreign interference, bullying and the law of the jungle should be rejected, he said. He added that major countries, in particular, should "take the lead in observing international norms and honoring the rule of law", and work together to tackle global challenges. "World affairs should be discussed by all, and international norms should be set by all. The authority and vitality of the UN need to be restored," Xi said. He also called for focusing on the development agenda, upholding openness and cooperation, and bridging the digital and artificial intelligence divides, so that the technological revolution and development achievements can benefit all nations. Xi said that after a 25-year journey, the SCO has successfully set a stellar example in conducting relations among big countries, among neighbors and among countries of different sizes. To advance common prosperity in the vast region straddling Asia and Europe, Xi called for harnessing "SCO Strength" and connecting multiple growth poles across the continent through high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. Xi also called on the SCO to promote the development and rise of the Global South through "SCO Wisdom", urging all sides to carry forward the Shanghai Spirit and strengthen and expand the SCO Plus partnerships. He said that "SCO Action" should guide the reform and improvement of global governance. Tuesday's meeting came exactly one year after Xi proposed the Global Governance Initiative at the SCO Plus Meeting in Tianjin. The initiative has since received support from nearly 160 countries and international organizations, while more than 60 countries have joined the Group of Friends of Global Governance. Li Yonghui, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of Russian, Eastern European and Central Asian Studies, said that the rise of the Global South and emerging economies is accelerating the shift toward a multipolar world. Li said that the SCO provides a practical example of cooperation among countries with different social systems and at different stages of development. zhaojia@chinadaily.com.cn

item.description:

Three words capture the SCO's vision: connectivity, pragmatism and autonomy Share - WeChat
The 2026 SCO Summit was held in Bishkek, the capital of the Kyrgyz Republic, from Aug 31 to Sept 1. In a recent interview with China Daily, Djoomart Otorbaev, former prime minister of the Kyrgyz Republic, said that connectivity goes far beyond roads and railways, embracing broader and multidimensional links; pragmatism enables cooperation among countries with different systems and national conditions into real results; and autonomy empowers the Global South to pursue independent development and shape its own future.
